To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effects of sarcoplasmatic reticulum calcium pump inhibitors in vascular smooth muscle of hypertensive rats were qualitatively similar to those observed in vascular smooth muscle from normotensive rats, and that the sensitivity of vascular smooth muscle cells from hypertensive rats was higher to the effects of the pump inhibitors.

the inhibition of Ca2+ transport by the sarcoplasmatic reticulum in smooth muscle cells from SHR and WKY rats causes a reduction of the contractile response to vasoconstrictors and inhibition of cell growth, but the effects are more pronounced in the SHR cells.

the inhibition of sarcoplasmatic reticulum calcium pump in vascular smooth muscles from SHR and WKY causes a similar decrease of transient contraction in Ca 2+-free medium and an increase of nifedipene-sensitive contraction on readmition of Ca 2+.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a possible mechanism of hypertension, namely, an impairment of calcium regulation in smooth muscle.
the role of the sarcoplamic reticulum Ca pump in vascular smooth muscles.
the role of Ca2+ in smooth muscle contraction and cell growth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of sarcoplasmatic reticulum Ca pump inhibitors on smooth muscle contraction and cell growth are common in both SHR and normotensive WKY rats.
a dysfunction of Ca2+ pumps in vascular smooth muscle may contribute, in part, to the development of hypertension in SHR.
the sarcoplasmatic Ca2+-ATPsase in vascular smooth muscle is not the only factor involved in the genesis of hypertension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a dysfunctional SR Ca2+ pump is a contributing factor for hypertension and that it can explain some of the vascular abnormalities associated with hypertension, such as enhanced vascular reactivity and vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation.
the dysfunctioning of Ca(2+)-pump ATPase in the SR is a contributing factor for development of genetic hypertension in SHR.

sarcoplasmic Ca2+ ATPase is a key enzyme for regulating Ca2+ homeostasis in the sarcoplamic reticulum in the vascular smooth muscle cells and its impairment in SHR is one important mechanism for the elevated cytosolic free Ca2+ concentration and the enhanced cell growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
thapsigargin is a useful pharmacological tool for studying the role of the Ca2+ pump.

the inhibition of sarcoplasm reticulum Ca-ATPase by thapsigargin or cyclopiazonic in aortic smooth muscles of spontaneously hypertensive rat and WKY rat resulted in a similar effect in the contraction in Ca2+ -free medium and in the inhibition of cell attachment and proliferation in cultured aortic muscle.
inhibition of the sarcoplastic reticulum calcium pump in vascular smooth muscles elicits a variety of effects that may contribute to the development of hypertension.
